questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13973094/assets/cac89f66c8c1e5e0ac6a9857cb7db48d3ca6edc2a83fb2ba3a63b0809cfe6ab0.png)

What is the $y$-intercept of the parabola shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the equation of the parabola. From the diagram, we see that the parabola has a vertex at $(5,-4)$ and passes through the point $(2,5).$

The general standard equation of an up- or down-opening parabola with vertex at $(h,k)$ is given by

$$
(x-h)^{2}=4p(y-k),
$$

and substituting $(h,k)=(5,-4)$ into the above gives

$$
(x-5)^{2}=4p(y+4).
$$

Now, we need to find $p.$ Since the parabola passes through the point $(2,5),$ we substitute $x=2$ and $y=5$ into the equation and get

$$
\begin{aligned}(2-5)^{2} & =4p(5+4) \\ 9 & =4p(9) \\ p & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the parabola is

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-5)^{2} & =y+4.\end{aligned}
$$

When the parabola intersects the $y$-axis, we must have $x=0.$ So, we substitute $x=0$ into the equation of the parabola and solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(0-5)^{2} & =y+4 \\ 25 & =y+4 \\ y & =25-4 \\ y & =21\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $y$-intercept is $21.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13973094/assets/0a9d728a5927f380bbc88445c6a409974d94050040f23000cce50f70de436917.png)

What are the $x$-intercepts of the parabola shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the equation of the parabola. From the diagram, we see that the parabola has a vertex at $(-3,-1)$ and passes through the point $(-6,8).$

The general standard equation of an up- or down-opening parabola with vertex $(h,k)$ is given by

$$
(x-h)^{2}=4p(y-k).
$$

Substituting $(h,k)=(-3,-1)$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)^{2} & =4p(y+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find $p.$ Since the parabola passes through the point $(-6,8),$ we substitute $x=-6$ and $y=8$ into the equation and get

$$
\begin{aligned}(-6+3)^{2} & =4p(8+1) \\ 9 & =4p(9) \\ p & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the parabola is

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)^{2} & =(y+1).\end{aligned}
$$

When the parabola intersects the $x$-axis, we must have $y=0.$ So, we substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the parabola and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)^{2} & =(0+1) \\ x+3 & =\pm 1 \\ x & =\pm 1-3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $x$-intercepts are $-4$ and $-2.$

What is the $x$-intercept of the parabola shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the equation of the parabola. From the diagram, we see that the parabola has a vertex at $(-8,-3)$ and passes through the point $(-2,-6).$

The general standard equation of a left- or right-opening parabola with vertex $(h,k)$ is given by

$$
(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h).
$$

Substituting $(h,k)=(-8,-3)$ into the above gives

$$
(y+3)^{2}=4p(x+8).
$$

Now, we need to find $p.$ Since the parabola passes through the point $(-2,-6),$ we substitute $x=-2$ and $y=-6$ into the equation and get

$$
\begin{aligned}(-6+3)^{2} & =4p(-2+8) \\ 9 & =4p(6) \\ p & =\frac{3}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the parabola is

$$
\begin{aligned}(y+3)^{2} & =\frac{3}{2}(x+8).\end{aligned}
$$

When the parabola intersects the $x$-axis, we must have $y=0.$ So, we substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the parabola and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(0+3)^{2} & =\frac{3}{2}(x+8) \\ 9 & =\frac{3}{2}(x+8) \\ \frac{18}{3} & =x+8 \\ x & =6-8 \\ x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $x$-intercept is $-2.$

What are the $x$-intercepts of the parabola shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the equation of the parabola. From the diagram, we see that the parabola has a vertex at $(-1,-4)$ and passes through the point $(2,5).$

The general standard equation of an up- or down-opening parabola with vertex $(h,k)$ is given by

$$
(x-h)^{2}=4p(y-k).
$$

Substituting $(h,k)=(-1,-4)$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+1)^{2} & =4p(y+4).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find $p.$ Since the parabola passes through the point $(2,5),$ we substitute $x=2$ and $y=5$ into the equation and get

$$
\begin{aligned}(2+1)^{2} & =4p(5+4) \\ 9 & =4p(9) \\ p & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the parabola is

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+1)^{2} & =y+4.\end{aligned}
$$

When the parabola intersects the $x$-axis, we must have $y=0.$ So, we substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the parabola and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+1)^{2} & =0+4 \\ (x+1)^{2} & =4 \\ x+1 & =\pm \sqrt{4} \\ x+1 & =\pm 2 \\ x & =1,-3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $x$-intercepts are $1$ and $-3.$

The value of the $y$-intercept of the parabola shown above  is{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the equation of the parabola. From the diagram, we see that the parabola has a vertex at $(4,-6)$ and passes through the point $(-2,3).$

The general standard equation of an up- or down-opening parabola with vertex at $(h,k)$ is given by

$$
(x-h)^{2}=4p(y-k),
$$

and substituting $(h,k)=(4,-6)$ into the above gives

$$
(x-4)^{2}=4p(y+6).
$$

Now, we need to find $p.$ Since the parabola passes through the point $(-2,3),$ we substitute $x=-2$ and $y=3$ into the equation and get

$$
\begin{aligned}(-2-4)^{2} & =4p(3+6) \\ 36 & =4p(9) \\ p & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the parabola is

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-4)^{2} & =4(y+6).\end{aligned}
$$

When the parabola intersects the $y$-axis, we must have $x=0.$ So, we substitute $x=0$ into the equation of the parabola and solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(0-4)^{2} & =4(y+6) \\ 16 & =4(y+6) \\ 4 & =y+6 \\ y & =4-6 \\ y & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $y$-intercept is $-2.$
